source: Nutrition Research Evidence Tracker (Yitz), curated for muscle, weight loss and the foods at home

studies.finding: About 30% fewer heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths vs. a low-fat-advice diet. The 2013 paper was retracted for randomization errors and republished in 2018 with the same conclusion.
studies.takeaway: Use extra-virgin olive oil as your main fat; eat a handful of nuts most days, plus vegetables, legumes and fish.
studies.design: RCT; 7,447 high-risk adults aged 55–80, Spain; median 4.8 yrs

studies.finding: The highest fiber eaters had 15–30% lower all-cause and cardiovascular death, coronary heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes and colorectal cancer. Benefits start at 25–29 g/day.
studies.takeaway: Aim for 25–29 g+ fiber a day from whole grains, beans, lentils, vegetables and whole fruit.
studies.design: Systematic review & meta-analysis; 185 cohort studies (135M person-years) + 58 trials

studies.finding: ≥3 g/day of oat beta-glucan lowered LDL by 0.25 mmol/L and total cholesterol by 0.30 mmol/L, with no effect on HDL or triglycerides.
studies.takeaway: About 1.5 cups of cooked oatmeal, or oats plus barley, gives roughly 3 g of beta-glucan.
studies.study: Whitehead et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2014

studies.finding: Going to ~6 servings a day raised gut-bacteria diversity and lowered 19 inflammatory markers, including IL-6. The high-fiber group showed no change in those markers.
studies.takeaway: Add yogurt, kefir, kimchi, sauerkraut or miso daily.

studies.finding: People ate ~500 kcal/day more on the ultra-processed diet and gained ~2 lb in 2 weeks; they lost ~2 lb on the unprocessed diet. The diets were matched for calories, sugar, fat and fiber.
studies.takeaway: Cook mostly from whole ingredients; limit packaged snacks, sugary drinks and processed meats.
studies.design: Inpatient crossover RCT; 20 adults; 2 weeks per diet

studies.finding: Protein increased strength and muscle gains from resistance training. There was no further gain above ~1.6 g/kg/day. It helped less with age and more in trained people.
studies.takeaway: If you lift: about 1.6 g protein per kg body weight a day, spread over meals. Food works; supplements are optional.
studies.study: Morton et al., Br J Sports Med 2018

studies.finding: A 6-hour eating window ending before 3 pm improved insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and oxidative stress, without weight loss.
studies.takeaway: A bigger breakfast/lunch and an earlier, lighter dinner may help blood sugar.
studies.design: Crossover controlled feeding RCT; 8 men with prediabetes; 5 weeks

studies.finding: Healthy low-fat and healthy low-carb diets gave similar weight loss at 12 months; genotype and insulin secretion did not predict who did better.
studies.takeaway: Pick the healthy pattern you can stick with; food quality matters more than the macro split.

studies.finding: Eating within an 8-hour window did not produce meaningful weight loss compared with three meals a day.
studies.takeaway: Eating windows aren't magic for weight; total intake matters.
studies.study: TREAT — Lowe et al., JAMA Intern Med 2020

studies.finding: Adding an 8 am–4 pm eating window to calorie restriction gave no significant extra weight loss over calorie restriction alone.
studies.takeaway: Calorie restriction drives weight loss; timing added little.

studies.finding: Eating breakfast did not help weight loss; breakfast eaters consumed ~260 more calories a day.
studies.takeaway: Eat breakfast if you enjoy it, but it isn't a weight-loss tool.

studies.finding: Eating later in the day increased hunger, lowered calories burned and shifted fat-tissue gene activity toward fat storage.
studies.takeaway: Shift meals earlier when you can.

studies.finding: Mortality was lowest with 50–55% of calories from carbs. Low-carb diets were linked to higher mortality when animal-based and lower mortality when plant-based.
studies.takeaway: If you eat lower-carb, use plant fats and proteins.
studies.study: ARIC + meta-analysis — Seidelmann et al., Lancet Public Health 2018

studies.finding: High-glycemic-index diets were linked to more cardiovascular disease and death, especially in people with existing heart disease.
studies.takeaway: Choose slower carbs: beans, intact whole grains, vegetables.

studies.finding: 28 g/day of nuts was linked to ~21% lower cardiovascular disease and ~22% lower all-cause mortality.
studies.takeaway: About one small handful (28 g) a day.

studies.finding: More than ½ tablespoon of olive oil a day was linked to 19% lower total mortality vs. rarely or never.
studies.takeaway: Swap butter and margarine for olive oil.
studies.study: Guasch-Ferré et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2022

studies.finding: Up to one egg a day was not associated with higher cardiovascular disease risk.
studies.takeaway: An egg a day is fine for most people.

studies.finding: 1–2 servings of fatty fish a week was linked to ~36% lower risk of dying from heart disease; benefits outweigh mercury risks for most adults.
studies.takeaway: Eat fatty fish about twice a week.
studies.design: Systematic review of trials and cohorts

studies.finding: One serving of yogurt a day was linked to ~18% lower type 2 diabetes risk.
studies.takeaway: Plain yogurt is a good daily food.

studies.finding: 3–4 cups a day was associated with the lowest mortality and lower risk of several diseases; caution advised in pregnancy.
studies.takeaway: Moderate coffee is fine or beneficial for most people.

studies.finding: Drinking ≥2 cups of black tea a day was linked to 9–13% lower mortality.
studies.takeaway: Tea is a healthy drink choice.
studies.study: UK Biobank — Inoue-Choi et al., Ann Intern Med 2022

studies.finding: Two or more sugary drinks a day was linked to 21% higher mortality vs. less than one a month.
studies.takeaway: Replace soda with water, coffee or tea.

studies.finding: WHO advised against using non-sugar sweeteners for weight control, citing no long-term benefit and possible risks.
studies.takeaway: Diet drinks aren't a weight-loss strategy; water is best.

studies.finding: 90 g/day of whole grains was linked to 17% lower all-cause mortality and 19% lower coronary heart disease.
studies.takeaway: About three servings a day (oats, brown rice, whole-wheat bread).

studies.finding: 5 servings a day (2 fruit + 3 vegetables) was linked to 13% lower mortality; starchy vegetables and fruit juice didn't add benefit.
studies.takeaway: Two fruits and three vegetables daily, favoring greens, citrus and berries.

studies.finding: Eating blueberries and strawberries ≥3 times a week was linked to ~32% lower heart-attack risk in young and middle-aged women.
studies.takeaway: Add berries several times a week.
studies.study: Nurses' Health Study II — Cassidy et al., Circulation 2013

studies.finding: Cocoa extract didn't significantly lower total cardiovascular events but was linked to 27% fewer cardiovascular deaths.
studies.takeaway: Not a reason to eat lots of chocolate; the evidence is for a flavanol extract.
studies.study: COSMOS — Sesso et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2022

studies.finding: UPF intake was linked to 32 health outcomes; the strongest evidence was for cardiovascular death, type 2 diabetes and common mental disorders.
studies.takeaway: Cutting ultra-processed foods is one of the most broadly supported changes.

studies.finding: About one serving a day of beans, lentils, chickpeas or peas lowered LDL cholesterol by ~5%.
studies.takeaway: Add a serving of legumes daily.

studies.finding: Adding pulses produced a small weight loss (~0.34 kg over ~6 weeks) even without calorie restriction.
studies.takeaway: Beans and lentils help fill you up.
studies.study: Kim et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2016

studies.finding: The highest fried-food intake was linked to ~28% higher major cardiovascular events vs. the lowest.
studies.takeaway: Limit deep-fried foods.

studies.topic: Whole fruit vs. fruit juice & diabetes
studies.finding: Whole fruits, especially blueberries, grapes and apples, were linked to lower type 2 diabetes risk; fruit juice was linked to higher risk.
studies.takeaway: Eat fruit whole rather than as juice.

studies.finding: Drinking 500 ml of water before each meal led to ~2 kg more weight loss over 12 weeks in older adults on a diet.
studies.takeaway: A glass or two of water before meals may help with appetite.
studies.design: RCT; 48 middle-aged and older adults; 12 weeks

studies.finding: Higher-protein, calorie-restricted diets produced slightly more weight and fat loss and better preservation of lean mass.
studies.takeaway: Keep protein up when cutting calories.
studies.study: Wycherley et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012

studies.finding: Replacing animal protein with plant protein was linked to lower mortality, especially when it replaced processed red meat.
studies.takeaway: Swap some meat for beans, lentils, tofu or nuts.
studies.study: Song et al., JAMA Intern Med 2016

studies.finding: Coffee didn't increase extra beats from the upper heart chambers; it slightly increased ones from the lower chambers, raised daily steps and cut sleep by ~36 minutes.
studies.takeaway: Coffee is generally safe for heart rhythm; avoid it late if it hurts your sleep.
studies.design: Randomized crossover trial; 100 adults; wearable monitoring

studies.finding: Each 50 g/day of processed meat was linked to 42% higher coronary heart disease and 19% higher diabetes; unprocessed red meat wasn't linked to heart disease.
studies.takeaway: Processed meat is the main concern.

studies.finding: Cutting free sugars led to ~0.8 kg weight loss and adding them ~0.75 kg gain; swapping sugar for other carbs at equal calories changed nothing.
studies.takeaway: Sugar adds weight mainly through extra calories.

studies.finding: Mediterranean and low-carb diets gave more weight loss than low-fat over 2 years; low-carb gave the best lipids and Mediterranean the best blood sugar in people with diabetes.
studies.takeaway: Mediterranean and low-carb are both effective options.

studies.finding: Larger portions and packages consistently made people eat more.
studies.takeaway: Serve smaller portions and use smaller packages.

studies.finding: Fast eaters had about twice the odds of obesity of slower eaters.
studies.takeaway: Slow down; put your fork down between bites.
studies.study: Ohkuma et al., Int J Obesity 2015

studies.finding: Higher protein intake did not harm kidney function in healthy adults.
studies.takeaway: Healthy people need not fear higher protein; people with kidney disease should follow their doctor.

studies.finding: Total daily protein, not eating it right after a workout, explained muscle gains.
studies.takeaway: Hit your daily protein total; the 'anabolic window' matters less.

studies.finding: Protein supplements increased gains in lean mass and strength from resistance training in both younger and older adults.
studies.takeaway: Pair strength training with enough protein.
studies.study: Cermak et al., Am J Clin Nutr 2012

studies.finding: Each daily serving of white rice was linked to ~11% higher type 2 diabetes risk, more so in Asian populations who eat more of it.
studies.takeaway: Swap some white rice for brown rice or other whole grains.
